about: Lab examples: each takes a published superintelligence idea, restates it in our own words (no copied text, no claims attributed to people), reproduces it as a deterministic toy experiment, then adds a hypothesis of ours as a variant with a stated prediction. Results are toy-scale: they test whether the idea's logic holds in a small model, not whether the original paper is right. Test data is synthetic. Edit freely; ids are kebab-case (docs/NAMING.md).

examples.title: Does self-improvement compound into an explosion?
examples.idea: If each generation of an AI system is better at building the next one, improvements feed on themselves, and capability could grow faster than exponentially: an "intelligence explosion".

reproduce.expect: With full compounding (returns = 1) capability grows exponentially and reaches 10x quickly.

hypothesis.statement: Ours: real AI research has diminishing returns to capability and a share of work (compute, experiments, data) that capability can't speed up. With returns of 0.6 and a 50% bottleneck, growth stays well short of exponential: reaching 10x takes more than twice as long.

examples.title: Can a decision-maker improve itself by writing its own tests?
examples.idea: A system that generates its own practice problems, checks its answers against feedback, and retrains on its mistakes can bootstrap better behaviour without new human labels. Repeating the loop is a small, safe form of recursive self-improvement.

reproduce.expect: Trained once on 30 requests, the policy handles familiar wording but misses requests phrased in new ways.

hypothesis.statement: Ours: eight rounds of writing 40 of its own test requests, learning from the failures and keeping a round only if held-out accuracy doesn't drop (a ratchet), raise held-out accuracy by at least 20 points while every safety property still holds.

examples.title: What happens to self-improvement without a ratchet?
examples.idea: Automated research loops keep a change only when a fixed measurement says it helped. That check is meant to make unattended self-improvement move in one direction instead of drifting.

reproduce.expect: With an imperfect self-check (30% of its own corrections carry the wrong label), the ratchet keeps only rounds that don't lower held-out accuracy. Averaged over 10 seeds, because one seed can point either way.

hypothesis.statement: Ours: with that noisy self-check, switching the ratchet off (keeping every round, mislabelled corrections included) ends with lower held-out accuracy than the ratchet.

examples.title: Optimising a proxy: Goodhart's law, and auditing as a fix
examples.idea: When a system is optimised hard against a measurable proxy for what we want, it eventually finds ways to raise the proxy that don't serve, or actively hurt, the real goal.

reproduce.expect: The proxy keeps rising while the true goal falls: a large proxy-minus-true gap.

hypothesis.statement: Ours: auditing just 20% of the optimiser's steps against the true goal (rejecting audited steps that hurt it) keeps the true goal from collapsing, cutting the gap by more than half.

examples.title: Can a weak supervisor train a stronger student?
examples.idea: As systems surpass their overseers, supervision gets weaker than the student. A capable student trained on a weaker supervisor's imperfect labels can still end up more accurate than that supervisor, because it learns the underlying pattern rather than the mistakes.

reproduce.expect: The student, trained only on noisy supervisor labels, beats the supervisor's own accuracy.

hypothesis.statement: Ours: dropping the 20% of labels the supervisor is least confident about (near the decision boundary, where it errs most) raises the student's accuracy further.

examples.title: Scaling laws, and what happens when data runs out
examples.idea: Test loss falls smoothly, roughly as a power law, as models get bigger, which is why progress can be forecast from compute and model size.

reproduce.expect: With plenty of data, loss falls steadily as a power law across all sizes tried.

hypothesis.statement: Ours: with only 50 training examples, bigger models stop helping early: the curve flattens at a smaller size and the best loss is worse. Forecasts from size alone break when data is the bottleneck.
